segments.text: Well, you're not alone. Many people find it hard to remember things they've read or learned,

segments.speaker: Georgina
segments.text: while other, sometimes useless, information sticks with them.

segments.text: whether that's someone's name, a word in English or where you put your wallet.

segments.text: But first, let me ask you my quiz question, Rob, before I forget.

segments.text: You and I might struggle to remember someone's phone number,

segments.text: Dr Jared Horvath is an educational neuroscientist at the University of Melbourne.

segments.speaker: Georgina
segments.text: According to him, there are two rules which explain how we remember information.

segments.speaker: Dr Jared Horvath
segments.text: Rule number one is repetition is key.

segments.speaker: Dr Jared Horvath
segments.text: The odds of remembering something after a one-off are incredibly slim.

segments.speaker: Dr Jared Horvath
segments.text: unless you can immediately link it to something you already understand.

segments.speaker: Dr Jared Horvath
segments.text: So my middle name is Cooney.

segments.speaker: Dr Jared Horvath
segments.text: If I ever meet someone named Cooney, I'll never forget that

segments.speaker: Dr Jared Horvath
segments.text: So a one-off is we all pretty much suck at it unless we focus.

segments.speaker: Dr Jared Horvath
segments.text: So rule two then becomes we remember what we focus on.

segments.text: The first rule for remembering is repetition.

segments.speaker: Georgina
segments.text: The odds, meaning the probability of remembering something,

segments.speaker: Georgina
segments.text: are low if you learn it as a one-off.

segments.speaker: Georgina

segments.speaker: Rob
segments.text: Dr Horvath's second rule is about focus.

segments.text: This involves making links between your information and something you already understand

segments.text: Ah yes, staying up late, trying to revise everything

segments.text: forget around 90% of what they studied within 72 hours.

segments.text: He thinks education shouldn't be about trying to cram students' heads with facts and figures.

segments.text: It should involve something more meaningful, as he explains to BBC World Service's The Y Factor.

segments.text: And the thing that I like about education is it's really moving from a model of

segments.speaker: Dr Jared Horvath
segments.text: just memorise as much as you can into what we now call deep learning,

segments.text: which is instead of giving you 100 things and I just need to know that you can remember them,

segments.text: I'm going to give you 10 things and instead of just being able to remember them,

segments.speaker: Dr Jared Horvath
segments.text: I want you to be able to describe it deeply and come up with new ways of looking at it.

segments.text: Traditionally, education involves memorising,

segments.text: learning information exactly as it is so you can repeat it later.

segments.text: But being able to repeat something like a parrot doesn't always mean you understand it.
